checks.label: When you think of coordinates as scalars, the basis arrows are what those scalars actually scale: on the first screen her numbers scale her two arrows, nose to tail, to the same tip that your numbers reach with i and j

Different coordinate systems are just different ways of representing the same vector: wherever either of her arrows is dragged, the arrow drawn keeps its tip, her How chain still ends on it, and only her numbers change

Going from her numbers to yours is matrix-vector multiplication, with a matrix whose columns represent Jennifer's basis vectors: the card shows P with her two arrows as its columns wherever they are dragged, and P times her numbers gives yours

Every worked number is right: P(2, 1) = (3, 3) and 2b₁ = (4, 2); determinant 3, and P⁻¹ = [1 1; −1 2] ÷ 3 takes (3, 3) to (6, 3) ÷ 3 = (2, 1); P(3, 3) = (3, 6) and 3b₁ + 6b₂ = (0, 9); (1, 2) lands on (0, 3), rows for columns on (4, 1); b₁ = (1, 1) gives (3, 0); (1, −1) is (0, −1) and P(1, −1) = (3, 0); the turn takes (3, 3) to (−3, 3) and her (2, 1) to (0, 3); P⁻¹MP = [3 0; 0 2]; (4, 2) is (3, 1) and P(4, 2) = (6, 2); area 0 for (2, 1) and (4, 2); 12 m is 4 lengths of 3 m; the worked example gives (1, 2) with determinant 5
Each puzzle's answer comes from the rule, and each wrong answer offered is the slip its hint names
Each puzzle offers three different answers, accepts only the right one, and draws every wrong one in the warning colour
Before Check, no puzzle shows its answer; after a right answer, it does

Each demonstration ends where the lesson says: the arrow (3, 3) read as (2, 1); b₁ on (1, 1) with her numbers (3, 0) and the arrow unmoved; P = [2 −1; 1 1] taking (2, 1) to (3, 3); a cell of area 3 and P⁻¹ = [1 1; −1 2] ÷ 3; the strip (2, 1), (3, 3), (−3, 3), (0, 3); the stretches to (3, 0) and (−2, 2) with P⁻¹MP = [3 0; 0 2]

While b₁ swings to (1, 1), the How chain re-lays along it and ends on the arrow's tip at every moment; while the arrow turns, its length stays the same; the product is written right to left, P first and P⁻¹ last
With her two arrows on one line, the cells have area 0: there is no How chain, her numbers read none (or many, when the arrow lies on that line), and P has no inverse
Every demonstration has finished arriving within its 3 to 4.5 s, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 2.5 s
